fullText: Most operating systems just help you check email or play games. But some have a much darker story behind them. Government surveillance built into the file system. Lawsuits worth millions over a single name. Even a system built by one man who believed God gave him the instructions. These are real cases documented by researchers and courts, not internet legends. Let's go through nine of them from the most disturbing to the most misunderstood. RedStar OS. Redstar OS is the official governmentissued operating system of North Korea. On the surface, it looks almost exactly like Mac OS with the same icons, the same dock, and the same general layout. If you saw a screenshot without context, you might think it was an Apple product. But underneath that familiar interface, it works in a completely different way. RedStar OS quietly adds an invisible digital watermark to every single file you open from a USB drive. This isn't limited to programs you run. It happens with documents, videos, music files, almost anything you plug in. The watermark happens automatically in the background, even if you never actually open the file at all. Just inserting the USB drive can be enough. The purpose of that watermark is tracking. It lets the government trace exactly who has been sharing or storing fobies, foreign music, or foreign books, all of which are illegal to access in North Korea. If a user notices the monitoring behavior and tries to disable it, the computer doesn't just block the action. It automatically restarts itself to undo the change and reenable tracking. Two German researchers, Florian Grunau and Nicklaus Shias, reverse engineered Red Star OS in detail and presented their findings publicly at the Chaos Communication Congress in 2015, confirming these surveillance features were real and intentional design choices, not bugs. The trade-off here isn't about speed or battery life or performance, the way it normally is with most tech comparisons. It's about complete loss of privacy built directly into the operating system from the ground up. This isn't software designed to serve the user sitting in front of the screen. It's software designed to serve the state watching that user from somewhere else entirely. Templeos Temple OS tells a very different kind of story. It's not illegal anywhere in the world and no government has ever banned it. Some companies simply don't allow it on internal machines, but that's only because it's technically outdated and has no real internet networking support, not because of any legal restriction. What makes Temple OS unforgettable isn't a law or a court case. It's the story of the person who built it. Temple OS was created entirely by one programmer, Terry A. Davis. Over more than 10 years of continuous obsessive work, Terry believed he had been instructed by God to build a modern version of the third temple, except in operating system form instead of physical stone and architecture. He didn't just write some code on top of an existing system either. He built the entire kernel from scratch, his own custom compiler, and even his own programming language called Holy C, all by himself without a team. Terry lived with schizophrenia for most of his adult life. And that ongoing struggle is deeply woven into the project's history, its strange visuals, and its unconventional design choices. This isn't a story about danger, crime, or surveillance like the previous entry. It's a story about obsession, isolation, raw talent, and someone fighting his own mind every single day while still managing to finish something most professional teams never would. That's exactly why so many programmers and tech historians still talk about Temple OS with genuine respect today rather than treating it as a joke. Livveness to Lin Spear, Lindows is a textbook example of a legal fight, not a security threat or a piece of dangerous software. The original goal behind Lindows was actually pretty simple and reasonable. Let regular people run Windows style applications on top of a Linux foundation, combining the openness of Linux with the familiarity of Windows software. But here's the twist. Microsoft didn't sue over the underlying technology at all. They sued specifically over the name. Linds sounded close enough to Windows that Microsoft's legal team considered it trademark infringement, something that could confuse customers in stores. The case dragged on for a while, but eventually Microsoft decided settling was smarter than continuing to fight it in court. They paid the company behind Lindo's close to $20 million to settle the dispute. And as part of that deal, Microsoft also bought the trademark rights to the name Lindo owes outright back in 2004. After the settlement, the project didn't disappear. It simply rebranded itself as Lindspire and kept developing from there. The trade-off in this entire story has nothing to do with malware, hacking, or stolen code. It's purely about trademark law. A single product name, four extra letters away from Windows, was enough to trigger a multi-million dollar legal battle, even though the actual software itself never did anything technically wrong or harmful to users. Reactose React OS is an open-source project with an ambitious goal. recreate the way Windows behaves completely from scratch without copying or using any of Microsoft's actual proprietary source code. That goal alone puts the project in a legally sensitive position from the very first line of code written. Back in 2006, the React OS development team made a serious decision. They froze all active development for several months, stopping new code contributions completely. Why take such a drastic step? The leadership became worried that some contributors, even unintentionally, may have looked at leaked Windows source code at some point while writing parts of React OS. If that turned out to be true, it could legally contaminate the entire codebase, opening the door to a massive lawsuit from Microsoft. So instead of taking that risk, the team paused everything and conducted a full internal audit, checking line by line where every piece of code actually came from. The trade-off here is pretty clear once you think about it. Building software that closely mimics a major commercial product, even with completely good intentions and zero malicious goals, means constantly having to prove you never crossed a legal line somewhere along the way. React OS ultimately survived that internal audit and continued development afterward. But the monthsl long pause shows just how fragile open- source clone projects can really be when they sit this close to someone else's intellectual property. Tails and Wix. Tales and Wix are both completely legal privacy tools, not hacking software and not anything inherently criminal. Both route your internet traffic through tour, a network designed to hide your real identity and physical location while browsing online. Because of that anonymity feature, people online often casually nickname them dark web operating systems, which sounds dramatic and a little scary. But that nickname genuinely misses the bigger, more important picture. Journalists around the world use these exact tools to protect confidential sources who could face serious danger if identified. Human rights activists living unsafe or authoritarian countries use them daily to avoid government tracking and surveillance. Edward Snowden, one of the most famous whistleblowers in modern history, has publicly confirmed using tools like these himself. The same anonym that can protect criminals trying to hide also protect whistleblowers, journalists, and ordinary people who are genuinely in danger because of what they know or what they're trying to expose. The trade-off is speed. Plain and simple. Routing every bit of your traffic through multiple layers of encryption and relay servers makes browsing noticeably slower than normal. For everyday tasks like checking email or watching videos, that slowdown usually isn't worth the hassle. But for someone whose physical safety genuinely depends on staying anonymous online, that tradeoff can matter more than almost anything else in their entire digital life. Kali Linux and Parrot OS. Kali Linux and Parrot OS are completely legal too and in fact they're actively taught inside schools and universities as part of cyber security courses. Both operating systems are specifically built for penetration testing which simply means finding security weaknesses inside a system before real malicious attackers manage to find them first. Companies around the world legally hire cyber security professionals who use exactly these tools to test their own internal networks with full permission and a signed contract beforehand. Just downloading Kali Linux onto your laptop is not a crime in any country. Nothing about possessing the software itself breaks any law. The moment it actually becomes illegal is when someone uses the tools inside it to break into a system they don't own and were never given permission to test in the first place. The operating system itself is completely neutral, almost like a toolbox sitting in a garage. It's the same kind of tool a locksmith uses and also the same kind of tool a burglar could misuse. What ultimately turns it into a crime isn't the software at all. It's entirely about how someone decides to use it and on whose systems they decide to point it. Pirated windowed be. Now, here's the one entry on this entire list that's actually illegal in a simple, direct, no gray area kind of way. Cracked or pirated Windows builds, sometimes nicknamed ghost builds in certain online communities, are unauthorized copies of Windows distributed for free, usually bypassing the official activation and licensing system entirely. This is straightforward copyright infringement. No complicated legal argument needed to explain it. But honestly, the legal risk isn't even the scariest part here. The bigger danger is what's frequently hidden inside these builds without the user ever knowing. These pirated versions are commonly packed with hidden malware, spyware, or secret back doors that the original uploader can access and control remotely, completely invisible to the average user installing it. Multiple real world organizations, including some government offices, have been seriously compromised after installing pirated Windows versions on official machines without realizing what extra software had been bundled silently inside the installer. The trade-off here is simple and honestly a little scary once you understand it fully. You save some money upfront by skipping the official license, but in exchange, you genuinely have no idea who else might have ongoing access to your system afterward. Sometimes for months or years without you ever noticing anything wrong. This is the one entry on this entire list where the warning isn't just historical or theoretical. It's something people are actively running into right now today in homes and offices around the world. Harmonyos. Harmony OS is Huawei's own independently developed operating system built largely as a direct response to US trade restrictions that cut off Huawei's access to core Android services and Google's app ecosystem. Harmony OS itself isn't illegal anywhere in the world, and there's no law banning regular people from using it on their own devices. The real issue surrounding it is geopolitical tension, not any actual criminal activity. Some governments choose to restrict its use specifically inside critical infrastructure systems or sensitive government agencies worried about the theoretical possibility of hidden back doors connected back to the manufacturer or by extension back to a foreign government. It's worth being clear though there's no public confirmed proof of an actual backdoor existing inside harmony OS. The restriction many countries apply is based purely on caution and a general lack of trust, not on any confirmed technical evidence uncovered by researchers. The trade-off here is really about supply chain trust at a national level. When an entire country depends heavily on foreign-made software running inside its most critical systems, the biggest risk involved usually isn't even technical in nature. It's fundamentally about political trust or the lack of it between competing governments. Neocyin and KY Lin OS. NeoKylin, also commonly known simply as Kylin OS, is a Chinese-developed operating system that visually looks strikingly similar to Windows XP, almost like a near identical recreation of that familiar early 2000s interface. It's used extensively inside Chinese government offices and military computer systems across the country. The core motivation behind building it is national independence, specifically reducing reliance on Americanmade software for operating the country's most critical national systems. This isn't an illegal operating system by any normal legal definition you could apply anywhere. It's fundamentally a national technology strategy, not a crime. Many other countries around the world are now actively building their own custom operating systems for this exact same underlying reason to avoid becoming permanently dependent on software entirely controlled by decision makers in another country. The trade-off involved is mainly development cost and somewhat slower software updates compared to mainstream global operating systems, but that's accepted in exchange for not being dependent on a single foreign company's business decisions or political pressure from another government down the line. So, out of all nine operating systems, most of them aren't illegal once you dig into the details. Some are legal tools that just carry a bad reputation like Tails or Kali Linux. Others are legal disputes over names or code like Lindows and React OS. Only one entry, pirated Windows builds, is actually straightforward copyright crime. And ironically, it's also the one most likely to quietly infect your own PC right now. Anyway, I've got more videos breaking down tech myths like this one. Go check them out. Okay.
